fields.description: One nav and one heatmap viewer for a growing analytics portal.
fields.intro: Heatmap is an analytics tool that shows online stores where visitors click and scroll, with screen recordings, site speed and AI insights. As a product design intern at Full Sprint, a design studio, I redesigned most of Heatmap’s portal.
fields.summary: Redesigning Heatmap’s analytics portal: one nav, a tabbed heatmap viewer, a place for AI insights and recordings beside their list.
fields.overview: Heatmap is for small businesses that sell online. It was a client of Full Sprint, where I was one of a few design interns; a colleague designed the AI insight cards. After I left, the redesign went through more iterations and was built on my designs.
fields.impact: Built after my internship, on my designs: 10x easier navigation, 4x faster load times and higher product ROI.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.heading: How might we bring Heatmap’s scattered new features into one portal that can keep growing?

children.text: Heatmap was a growing product, and new features kept arriving. By the summer of 2024, the tools around its heatmaps (scrollmaps, a data table, screen recordings, site speed and AI) were scattered across the portal and felt bolted on. The redesign set out to pull them together and leave room for whatever came next.

In the old viewer, you picked a page from a URL dropdown, opened the data table from a separate button and switched map types in a dropdown on the other side. The dashboard already had an AI Insights column in one table, and also listed AI Insights under “Upcoming Features”, next to a Chrome extension and split testing.

content.caption: The portal before the redesign.

images.alt: The old Heatmap viewer: a URL dropdown at the top, Data table, 30 days, Add filter and Create Custom Box buttons, desktop, mobile and tablet icons and a Clickmap dropdown above a store page with heat spots
images.label: Viewer

images.alt: The old Heatmap dashboard, scrolled down: average site speed, rage clicks, a device type chart and an Upcoming Features card listing AI Insights, Chrome Extension and Split Testing
images.label: Dashboard

children.text: Who:
small businesses that sell online.
Where:
a desktop web portal.
Timeframe:
two summer months.

Other analytics tools face the same challenge: lots of features, and one place to find them all. Before designing anything, I looked at how they handle it, then went through Heatmap’s own portal, mapping where every feature lived and how you got from one to the next.
The competitive audit covered Amplitude, Sprig, June, Plausible and PostHog, grouped by navigation, dashboards, heatmaps and data, and video playback.

content.alt: A competitive audit board with screenshots of Amplitude, Sprig, June, Plausible and PostHog, grouped under Navigation, Dashboard, Heatmap/Data and Video Playback
content.caption: The competitive audit, one board per part of the portal.

children.text: Three patterns kept coming up:

notes.text: Split views that show data alongside a list

children.text: What the portal audit found
Scattered features:
related insights lived in separate, unconnected places.
Inconsistent patterns:
new features brought their own buttons, cards and icons.
Navigation bottlenecks:
switching heatmap views or applying a filter took several steps.
No room to grow:
the structure wasn’t built for more features.

For the look, I didn’t start from scratch. Heatmap already had a public preview page, approved by stakeholders, with a newer colour palette and type, and I carried that style through the whole portal.

sections.title: Navigation
sections.heading: A nav with room to grow

children.text: Every tool in Heatmap is one click away from the nav, and it’s where I started, on paper. It had to hold today’s pages, a list of the pages you care about, and space for features that didn’t exist yet.
I sketched two structures: a nav column that runs the full height of the window, and a nav card that sits under a full-width top bar.

content.caption: My two structures. On the second, the top bar is where “actions can be placed”.

images.alt: A notebook sketch of a full-height navigation column with notes: 16px radius, secondary navigation, expand/collapse navbar, rounded nav column, full height nav, knocked out colours
images.label: Full-height nav

images.alt: A notebook sketch of a nav card under a full-width top bar with notes: actions can be placed here, header or CTA, section dividers, and if CTA is present, where to locate expand button
images.label: Top bar and nav card

children.text: The top bar won. It gave the account and other global actions a home outside the nav, and it was what the team and the client preferred. The rounded nav column from the first sketch stayed.
Which list belongs in the nav
Under the main links, the nav holds a list of pages. Two more sketches asked what that list should be, and where adding a page fits.

content.caption: Add Page inside the list, and a list that swaps with the page.

images.alt: A notebook sketch of a nav with Add Page at the top and a page list, noting: maybe add page should be in the heatmaps pages list still
images.label: Add Page in the list

images.alt: A notebook sketch of a nav with panels for recently accessed, your heatmaps and screen recordings, noting: swappable instance based on page, dashboard to recents, heatmaps to heatmaps list, screen recordings to recents
images.label: A list for each page

children.text: In the sandbox, it took a few rounds:
a fixed Starred list, with View All.
a list that changes with the page, as in the sketch: Recently Accessed on the Dashboard, all your heatmaps on Heatmaps.
the same lists, with Add Page moved from the top of the nav into the list’s header.
Final:
starred heatmaps or starred recordings, with the full list on its own Heatmaps page (and Add New Page with it), and recents on the dashboard.

content.alt: Four versions of the Heatmap nav side by side: V1 with Add Page and a Starred list, V2 with Your Heatmaps, V3 with Welcome, Dylan and an add button in the list header, and the final nav with Starred Heatmaps
content.caption: V1, V2 and V3 from the nav sandbox, then the final nav on the Heatmaps page.

children.text: I came back to starring because the full list was cramped in the nav. Recents belong on the dashboard, and favourites stay in the nav. The nav also folds down to a rail of icons, with a chevron next to the greeting.
A note to myself
It would be better for the selected nav item’s icon to be a filled variant.
I left that sticky note next to my first version, then made the change: the page you’re on now gets a filled icon and green text.

content.caption: The selected Dashboard item in the sandbox, then with the filled icon.

images.alt: The sandbox nav with Dashboard selected, shown only by brighter text next to an outlined icon
images.label: Before

images.alt: The next nav with Dashboard selected, shown by a filled green icon and green text
images.label: After

children.text: Open a heatmap and there are three ways to read the same page: where people click, how far they scroll, and a table of numbers for every element on it. In the old portal those sat behind separate buttons and dropdowns, so I set out to build one viewer that held all three.
I tried the layouts side by side in a sandbox: a split view with the list next to the heatmap, a collapsed version of it, a full-page list, and tabs.

content.caption: Three of the sandbox layouts.

images.alt: A sandbox layout with the list of heatmaps in the nav next to a dark placeholder for the heatmap
images.label: Split

images.alt: A sandbox layout with a full-page table of heatmaps: title, URL, two metrics and revenue
images.label: List

images.alt: A sandbox layout with a back arrow, the page name and tabs for Heatmap, Scrollmap, Data Table and AI Insights above a heatmap of a supplement page
images.label: Tabs

children.text: The split view didn’t carry forward for heatmaps; it ended up in recordings instead. The full list moved out of the nav onto its own Heatmaps page, and the viewer got tabs: Heatmap, Scrollmap and Data Table became three views of one page, which made the structure clearer.

content.alt: The final Heatmap viewer with the nav collapsed: the title Heatmaps: Homepage, Heatmap, Scrollmap and Data Table tabs, device, date and filter controls, and a heatmap of the Jellybee home page
content.caption: The final viewer, with the nav folded into a rail.

children.text: Controls around the map
The controls that used to be spread around got fixed places:
The title is the page switcher.

Early versions had a “Back to list” link, then a back arrow, then a breadcrumb. From Iteration 1 the title read “Heatmaps: Homepage”, and by Iteration 3 clicking it opened a searchable table of your pages, so you can jump to another heatmap without leaving the viewer.
Devices became a segmented control,
with a count for desktop, tablet and mobile.
Date range and filters
sit next to them. Data Mode and Interactive Mode sit in a bar at the bottom, with Compare Data.

content.alt: The page switcher open under the title Heatmaps: Homepage: a date range, Add Filter and search above a table of pages with URL, metrics and revenue, with Landing Page TheJellyBee highlighted
content.caption: The page switcher, opened from the title.

children.text: The data table
Before, the data table slid over the page from a button. Now it’s a tab: the full table, with a preview of the page next to it, for mobile or desktop, that you can fold away.

content.caption: A slide-over, then a tab with its own preview.

images.alt: The old data table sliding over the left half of the page, with Featured and Deleted tabs and rows of sessions, purchases and revenue
images.label: Before

images.alt: The new Data Table tab: a full table of clicks, purchases, revenue and conversion rate for each element, with a mobile preview of the page on the right
images.label: After

children.text: Comparing visitors

Filters got their own system. You can filter by session data, like entry page, traffic source or rage clicks, or by e-commerce data, like purchasers or average order value. Or you can compare two groups, such as returning and new users. There are two ways in: through Add Filter, or straight from the Compare Data button.
The chips that show what you’re comparing changed too. I tried a filled pill first, then an underline like the main tabs. The next version added “+ Add Comparison”.

content.alt: Three versions of the compare chips: a filled pill for Total Pages Visited next to Non Purchasers, the same with an underline, and Purchasers, Non Purchasers and Add Comparison
content.caption: A pill, an underline, then room for more groups.
The filter and compare panels.

images.alt: The All Filters panel: session data, e-commerce data and custom filters, with Clear Filters, Compare and Apply
images.label: Filter

images.alt: The compare panel: Compare Returning Users to New Users, with the same filter lists and Clear Comparison and Compare buttons
images.label: Compare

children.text: AI was the newest arrival in Heatmap: Heatmap Insights give you AI-generated recommendations to improve your site, like “Shorten Button Text”. My colleague designed the insight cards and what they say. My part was deciding where they live in the viewer, and that took five tries.
In Iteration 1, insights sat behind a small sparkle icon at the bottom right. Iteration 2 gave it a label: “AI Insights”.

content.caption: A sparkle icon, then a labelled button, both at the bottom right.

images.alt: The viewer in Iteration 1, with a small sparkle icon button at the bottom right, after Data Mode and Interactive Mode
images.label: Iteration 1

images.alt: The viewer in Iteration 2, with a labelled AI Insights button at the bottom right
images.label: Iteration 2

children.text: Iteration 3 made AI Insights a fourth tab, next to Heatmap, Scrollmap and Data Table. In Iteration 4 the tab was gone, and a thin rail ran down the right edge with the sparkle at the top.

content.caption: A fourth tab, then a rail on the right edge.

images.alt: The viewer in Iteration 3, with AI Insights as a fourth tab after Heatmap, Scrollmap and Data Table
images.label: Iteration 3

images.alt: The viewer in Iteration 4, with no AI tab and a thin rail on the right edge holding a sparkle icon
images.label: Iteration 4

children.text: In the final version, that rail opens a Heatmap Insights panel, and folds back into the rail when you’re done.

Insights make sense next to the heatmap they’re about, and a panel lets you read both at once. They also aren’t a view of the data like the three tabs are. They’re advice, so they didn’t belong among them. Feedback from the team and the client led there too.

content.alt: The final Heatmap viewer with the nav expanded, a mobile heatmap of the Jellybee home page, and the Heatmap Insights panel open on the right with suggestions such as Shorten Button Text and Change Button Color
content.caption: The final viewer, with Heatmap Insights open next to the map.

children.text: Sometimes a heatmap isn’t enough and you want to watch what one visitor actually did. Screen recordings play back real sessions on your store. In the old portal, each recording opened on its own page, and you went “Back to Recordings” to find the next one.
Split views were one of the patterns from the audit, and this is where it stuck: the list on the left, the recording on the right with Previous and Next, and an Overview and Timeline underneath.

content.caption: A page for each recording, then the list and recording side by side.

images.alt: The old recording page: Back to Recordings, a video player with playback controls, an event timeline on the right and session info below
images.label: Before

images.alt: The new Screen Recordings page: a list of sessions on the left, the recording on the right with Previous and Next, and Overview and Timeline below it
images.label: After

children.text: Under the recording, I tried two layouts: Overview and Timeline side by side (Layout A), or the timeline as a strip above the Overview (Layout B). Layout A is the one in the final prototype.

content.caption: Layout A made it into the prototype.

images.alt: Screen recordings with Overview and Timeline side by side under the recording
images.label: Layout A

images.alt: Screen recordings with the Timeline as a horizontal strip above the Overview
images.label: Layout B

children.text: I also designed the in-between states: nothing selected yet, no starred recordings (“Add stars to get started”), and the list folded away so the recording gets the full width.

content.caption: An empty state, and the list folded away.

images.alt: Screen recordings with the list on the left and an empty viewer that says Select a recording to view it here
images.label: Nothing selected

images.alt: Screen recordings with the nav and list collapsed, so the recording, Overview and Timeline fill the width
images.label: List collapsed

children.text: Before you open a single heatmap, the dashboard gives you the big picture: whether tracking is live, a few key numbers, and how your pages are doing. I sketched it and wrote down why each detail was there.

content.alt: Four notebook pages of dashboard sketches, with notes on engaged sessions, site speed, page traffic and error messages with a Heatmap Translator
content.caption: My dashboard sketches, with notes on each detail.

children.text: The old dashboard already had most of the pieces: live snippet status, four key numbers with sparklines, page traffic, rage clicks and site speed. I kept them and worked on how they read. From my notes:
A dot at the end of each line
shows the data is live.
Green and red percentages
give a quick comparison with the previous day, week or month.
Visitors inline, larger titles and more defined rows
make the tables cleaner and the hierarchy clearer.
Tabs in the site speed card
switch between charts.
In Figma, a greybox came first: the key numbers and a new Recently Accessed table in full, with grey placeholders for everything below. The full design followed.

content.caption: The top of the dashboard, before and after the details went in.

images.alt: The dashboard greybox: key number cards and a Recently Accessed table above grey placeholder bars for page traffic, rage clicks and site speed
images.label: Greybox

images.alt: The full dashboard: LIVE snippet status, four key numbers with green and red changes, Recently Accessed, and page traffic and rage clicks under Site Performance
images.label: Full design

children.text: Further down, site speed got Data and Ratings views with suggestions beside the chart. Error Messages and the Heatmap Translator were features Heatmap already had, and I redesigned them too: each error’s raw console text sits next to the Translator’s plain-language explanation.

content.alt: The lower half of the dashboard: a Site Speed card with metrics, a chart and suggestions, and Error Messages with a list of errors, a terminal view and a Heatmap Translator explanation
content.caption: Site speed with suggestions, and an error explained by the Heatmap Translator.

children.text: Toward the end of my internship, I presented the high-fidelity prototype to the Full Sprint and Heatmap team. Behind it was a design system of 32 new components, and the prototype had over 300 interactions, from folding the nav to switching tabs and opening the filters.
The response was positive about the unified style and the simpler navigation.
After I left, there were more iterations on top of my designs, and then the redesign was built. The built redesign brought 10x easier navigation, 4x faster load times and higher product ROI.

content.alt: Overhead view of a laptop on a wooden desk with an apple and a notepad, showing the final Heatmap viewer with Heatmap Insights open

children.text: What I learned
Structure before polish.
Fixing the navigation and layout mattered more than restyling screens.
A system holds it together.
Components kept a big redesign consistent and easy to build on.
Summary

Heatmap kept adding features, and its portal showed it. As one of a few design interns at Full Sprint, I redesigned most of it: a nav under a top bar with starred lists, one viewer with tabs and a page switcher, a place for AI insights next to the heatmap, recordings beside their list, and a dashboard built around live numbers.
The redesign was built after my internship, on my designs, with 10x easier navigation and 4x faster load times.
